notes.claim: Integration is the inverse of differentiation: the two halves of the course undo each other.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency's second-engineer maths syllabus has a differentiation section and an integration section, so both halves are on Dan's route.
An HN Engineering Mathematics 2 unit (SQA, 40 notional hours) gives 10 hours to differentiation and 8 hours to integration.
Leibniz notation (dy/dx) is quite common in engineering and physics.
The same HN unit applies integration to engineering problems such as work done by an expanding gas, mean values and root mean square values.
The average rate of change over an interval is the ratio of the change in the function over that interval to the corresponding change in x.
The slope of a secant line (a line through two points on a curve) is used to estimate the rate at which one variable changes in relation to another.
The MCA second-engineer maths syllabus includes determining the gradient of a chord.
One calculus teacher (Bressoud, MAA) reports that at the start of Calculus I nearly everyone can compute an instantaneous rate, but almost no one gives the correct average rate of change.
The MCA second-engineer electro-technology syllabus writes an inductor's self-induced emf with changes, e = LΔi/Δt, so Δ as "change in" is already in Dan's papers.
As the second point moves toward the first, the secant line's slope becomes a better approximation to the rate of change of the function at that point.
Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity over a small time interval.
The instantaneous rate of change of a function is its derivative, the rate of change at any point along the function.
dy/dx is written from the limit of the difference in y-values divided by the difference in x-values; the MCA syllabus likewise defines dy/dx as the limiting value of δy/δx.
Textbooks build the derivative as a limit of secants, while one teacher argues students should not base the derivative on the tangent's slope.
notes.contested: OpenStax's calculus text recognises the tangent as the limit of secant lines, whereas Bressoud (MAA) argues students should not base their understanding of the derivative on the slope of the tangent.

notes.claim: For i2: at a sharp corner a function has no derivative, because the slopes from the left and from the right settle on different values (OpenStax's example is f(x) = |x| at 0).
The derivative function gives the derivative of a function at each point in its domain where the derivative is defined.
For f(x) = x² − 2x the derivative function is f′(x) = 2x − 2.
Applying the power rule d/dx of xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹ to x² gives 2x (our arithmetic from the rule).
Leibniz notation, such as dy/dx, is quite common for writing the derivative in engineering and physics.
The power rule: bring the power to the front, then subtract one from the power, so d/dx of xⁿ is nxⁿ⁻¹; the MCA syllabus covers ax^n for positive or negative n.
A derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant multiplier carries through.
Rules plus the power rule differentiate a polynomial term by term; for 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 that gives 12x² − 4x + 7 (our arithmetic from the rules).
The derivative of a constant function is zero.

The chain rule: the derivative of a composite function, one rule inside another, is the outer function's derivative at the inner function times the inner function's derivative (added for i4's optional chain-rule screen).
Instantaneous electrical current is the time derivative of the charge that flows, written i = dq/dt.
An ampere is one coulomb of charge per second, which is the unit of this rate.
Differentiating a position function at a given time gives the velocity at that time.
The current through a capacitor equals the capacitance times the rate of change of its voltage.
The MCA syllabus asks for velocity from displacement-time functions; the HN unit asks for the rate of change of a variable in an engineering problem.
Capacitance is charge per volt: one farad holds one coulomb for each volt across the plates (C = Q/V, so q = Cv). Added for i5 (review fix).
The voltage across an inductor is the derivative of the current through it, multiplied by its inductance in henrys (v = L di/dt). Added for i5 (review fix).
As a capacitor-style charge builds up to its maximum, its derivative, the current, decreases towards zero. Added for i5 (review fix: the charging sketch).
A function's derivative is zero where its graph has a horizontal tangent, at a turning point.
If a function has a local extremum at a point, that point is a critical point; a critical point is only a candidate and need not be a maximum or minimum.
On a closed interval, a largest or smallest value occurs either at an endpoint or at an interior point, where it is a local extremum and so at a critical point.
An HN engineering unit uses derivatives to locate turning points and to find the condition for maximum electrical power transfer.
Integration is the inverse of differentiation; add one to the power and divide by the new power.
Because inverse operations do the opposite in the opposite order, the power rule for integrals adds 1 to the power, then divides by it.
The power rule for integrals cannot be used at n = −1 because it would divide by n + 1 = 0.
The constant c appears because differentiating a constant gives zero; it is fixed from given conditions such as initial values.
SQA examiners report that candidates make basic errors in dealing with the constant of integration.
Adding the areas of rectangles under a rate graph approximates the total; the evaluation theorem then gets the exact area by evaluating an antiderivative at both ends and subtracting.
When a quantity changes, its new value equals its initial value plus the integral of its rate of change.
Integrating the current function over a time interval gives the charge transferred in that interval.
By the evaluation theorem, any antiderivative of the integrand will do when evaluating a definite integral.
An integral describes a quantity as a sum of many small pieces (MIT 18.01).
The definite integral can be taught as the area under a curve or as an accumulation of a rate.
notes.contested: Textbooks such as OpenStax define the definite integral by area under a curve, while physics-education researchers found students could say 'the integral equals the area' yet not link it to accumulation.

notes.claim: The MCA Applied Heat syllabus names the mid-ordinate rule, for finding the area of an indicator card.
The integral of p dV is the area under the pV curve, and the work done by the gas is positive for expansion and negative for compression.
The MCA Applied Heat syllabus says the area of the pV diagram represents work done and asks for the area under the curve given by pVⁿ = C.
A polytropic process is one in which pVⁿ = constant.
Work done on the system in a polytropic process is (p₂V₂ − p₁V₁) ÷ (n − 1); work by the gas has the opposite sign, (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1), the form given for an adiabatic process.
The same syllabus asks for the area of an indicator card by the mid-ordinate rule.
A gas expanding against a piston exerts a force through a distance and does work; the force is the pressure times the piston face area (for i9).
The MCA Applied Heat syllabus asks for mean effective pressure to be defined, and General Engineering Science II asks for it from indicator card data (for i9).
Mean effective pressure is defined as the net work divided by the displacement volume (for i9).
1 bar is 100 kPa (for i9, a unit conversion).
The average value of a function on an interval is its definite integral divided by the length of the interval.
RMS value: square the function, find the mean over a period, then take the square root.
For a sine wave the RMS value is the peak divided by the square root of 2, about 0.707 of the peak.
The mean of a sine wave over a whole cycle is zero, so its mean is taken over half a cycle, when it is 0.637 of the peak.
The RMS value is the steady DC value that would give the same energy to a circuit.
The MCA Marine Electro-technology syllabus asks for the mean value and rms value of a sine wave.
The a.c. produced by an alternator (an a.c. generator) follows the shape of a sine wave (i10).
The form factor of an a.c. waveform is its RMS value divided by its average value (i10).
